explain.body: “Some of these can be measured directly and indirectly using some tools and instruments such as length of an object using a ruler, time duration of an event using a clock, the temperature (the degree of hotness) of somebody using a thermometer. explain.title: SI helps everyone measure in a common way
explain.body: SI is the international system of units. Using it helps scientists share and compare observations and results easily.

explain.title: The seven base units
explain.body: The seven base units are metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), kelvin (K), ampere (A), candela (cd) and mole (mol). Their values are fixed with reference to international standards.

explain.title: Derived units come from base units

explain.title: What scientific notation means
explain.body: It is short way of representing very large or very small numbers. The numerical part of the quantity is written as a number from 1 to 9 multiplied by whole number powers of 10.

explain.title: Writing a large number
explain.body: To write numbers using scientific notation, move the decimal point until only one non-zero digit remains on the left. Count the places moved: moving the decimal to the left gives a positive exponent of 10. For example, 138,000,000 km = 1.38 × 10⁸ km.

explain.title: Writing a small number

explain.title: Least count
explain.body: Least count is the smallest measurement that can be taken accurately with an instrument. The metre rule's least count is 1 mm. In this section, Vernier Callipers has a least count of 0.1 mm and a micrometer screw gauge has a least count of 0.01 mm.

explain.title: Read the ruler from above
explain.body: Parallax error is due to incorrect position of eye when taking measurements. It can be avoided by keeping eye perpendicular to the scale reading. In Fig. 1.1, point B gives the correct reading.

explain.title: Vernier Callipers
explain.body: It is an instrument used to measure small lengths down to 1/10th of a millimetre. It can be used to measure the thickness, diameter, width or depth of an object. The two scales on it are: (a) A main scale which has marking of 1mm each. (b) A Vernier (sliding) scale of length 9 mm and it is divided into 10 equal parts.

explain.title: Zero error
explain.body: If the zeros of the main scale and Vernier scale do not exactly coincide when the jaws are joined, the instrument has zero error. A Vernier zero to the right of the main-scale zero reads slightly more, so subtract the zero error. A Vernier zero to the left reads slightly less, so add the zero error.

explain.title: Micrometer screw gauge
explain.body: A screw gauge measures very small lengths such as the diameter of a wire or the thickness of a metal sheet. Its least count is the pitch divided by the number of divisions on the circular scale.

Using the wrong correction direction for zero error: subtract for a Vernier zero to the right and add for a Vernier zero to the left.
Leaving out units or writing a reading with more precision than the instrument supports.

explain.body: “It is a cylinder made of glass or transparent plastic with a scale divided in cubic centimetres (cm³ or cc) or millilitres (mL) marked on it. explain.title: Meniscus and reading water
explain.body: “The meniscus is the top level of the liquid surface.” Water curves downward and its surface is called concave. For water, take the reading at the bottom edge of the surface. Mercury curves upward, making a convex surface, so take its reading at the top edge.

explain.body: Note the liquid reading before and after placing a non-dissolvable solid in it. The difference between the readings is the solid’s volume. modelAnswer: Human errors occur due to personal performance, such as difficulty estimating a pointer's position or reaction time when starting or stopping a clock.

explain.title: Measurements have errors
explain.body: Measurements using tools and instruments are never perfect. They can differ from their true values, so a scientific measurement should indicate the estimated error.

explain.title: Human errors
explain.body: “They occur due to personal performance.” Examples include difficulty reading a pointer, using a faulty procedure to read a scale, or reaction time when starting or stopping a clock. Training, proper technique and digital instruments can help reduce them.

explain.title: Systematic errors
explain.body: “They refer to an effect that influences all measurements of particular measurements equally.” A definite cause, such as zero error or poor calibration, produces a consistent difference in readings. Comparing with a more accurate instrument can help, and a correction factor can be applied.

explain.title: Random errors
explain.body: “It is said to occur when repeated measurements of a quantity give different values under the same conditions.” Unknown, unpredictable causes, including environmental changes, can produce them. Take several readings and use their average or mean to reduce their effect.

explain.title: Recognise the cause
explain.body: A personal reading or handling problem points to human error; a definite, consistent instrument effect points to systematic error; unpredictable variation between readings points to random error.

mistakes: Calling every incorrect reading a human error: first identify the cause of the error.
Mixing up systematic and random errors: systematic errors affect readings consistently, while random errors vary unpredictably.

writtenQuestions.text: Differentiate between precision and accuracy of a measurement with examples.
modelAnswer: Precision of a measurement refers to how close together a group of measurements actually are to each other.
Accuracy of a measurement refers to how close the measured value is to some accepted or true value.
Arrows clustered together away from the bullseye are precise but not accurate.
Arrows clustered at the bullseye are both accurate and precise.
Therefore, precision compares measurements with each other, while accuracy compares a measurement with the true value.

explain.body: Your textbook gives this rule: “If the number before the 5 is odd, one is added to the last digit retained. If the number before the 5 is even, it remains the same.” For example, 4.45 rounds to 4.4 at two significant figures, while 4.55 rounds to 4.6.

explain.title: Use the nearer value when needed
explain.body: Your textbook also explains that sometimes logic is applied to decide the fate of a digit. It gives 4.452 rounded to two significant figures as 4.5, because 4.452 is closer to 4.5 than to 4.4.

mistakes: Keeping too many or too few significant figures instead of the number requested.
Changing the retained digit when the next digit is less than 5.
Forgetting the odd/even rule when the next digit is exactly 5.
Changing or omitting the power of ten or the unit in the final answer.
Rounding 4.452 to 4.4 without considering the textbook's nearest-value explanation.

explain.title: Physical quantities and units
explain.body: A physical quantity can be measured and expressed using a number and a unit. Base quantities are independent; derived quantities are formed from base quantities. The SI base units are metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol) and candela (cd).

explain.title: Choosing instruments and reading them
explain.body: Choose an instrument suited to the size being measured. Vernier Callipers use a main scale and Vernier scale; a micrometer screw gauge is useful for very small thicknesses. Read scales with the eye level with the mark or meniscus to avoid parallax error.

explain.title: Prefixes and scientific notation
explain.body: Prefixes such as kilo, milli, micro and nano make very large or small quantities easier to write. Scientific notation writes a number as a coefficient from 1 to 10 multiplied by a power of 10.

explain.title: Significant digits and calculations
explain.body: Significant digits communicate the precision of a measurement. Leading zeros are not significant; zeros between non-zero digits and trailing decimal zeros are significant. In addition and subtraction, align powers of ten; in multiplication and division, combine powers.

explain.title: Errors, precision and accuracy
explain.body: Human errors come from the observer. Random errors vary unpredictably, while systematic errors create a consistent shift. Precision is agreement between repeated measurements; accuracy is closeness to the true value.

mistakes: Choosing an instrument that is too coarse for the size being measured.
Looking at a scale or meniscus from above or below, causing parallax error.
Writing a measurement without its unit or using a unit for the wrong quantity.
Adding or subtracting numbers in scientific notation before making their powers of ten the same.
Counting leading zeros as significant digits or ignoring a trailing decimal zero.
Forgetting to convert units before substituting into a formula, especially kilometres to metres or centimetres cubed to metres cubed.
Reporting an answer with unjustified precision or omitting the requested SI prefix.

notes.title: Physical and Non-Physical Quantities
notes.answer: A physical quantity can be measured; a non-physical quantity cannot be measured with tools and instruments.
notes.explanation: A physical quantity can be measured with tools or instruments. A non-physical quantity cannot be measured with tools and instruments; it may be described or compared using agreed criteria or surveys.
notes.simple: If you can measure it with an instrument and give its result as a number with a unit, it is a physical quantity. If you cannot, it is non-physical.
examples: Length is a physical quantity because it can be measured with a ruler.
Fear is a non-physical quantity because it cannot be measured with a measuring instrument.
steps: Ask whether the quantity can be measured with a tool or instrument.
If it can be measured, classify it as a physical quantity.
If it cannot be measured, classify it as a non-physical quantity.
For a physical measurement, state its numerical value and unit.
notes.checkQuestion: Does a non-physical quantity have dimensions?
notes.checkAnswer: No. A non-physical quantity cannot be measured with tools and instruments, so it has no measurable magnitude and unit.

notes.title: Base and Derived Quantities
notes.answer: Base quantities are chosen quantities used as a starting point. Derived quantities are described in terms of one or more base quantities. A measurement is a comparison with a standard and consists of a number and a unit.
notes.explanation: Base quantities are the chosen starting quantities. A derived quantity is described using one or more base quantities. Measurements compare an unknown quantity with a standard, and every measurement needs both a number and a unit.
notes.simple: Base quantities are the starting quantities. Derived quantities are made from them. A measurement needs a number and a unit.
examples: Distance and time are base quantities; speed depends on distance and time, so speed is derived.
Density is described in terms of mass and volume, so density is derived.
steps: Identify the quantity being described.
Check whether it is one of the chosen base quantities or is described using base quantities.
If it depends on one or more base quantities, call it a derived quantity.
For any measurement, include both the number and the unit.
notes.checkQuestion: Why is speed a derived quantity?
notes.checkAnswer: Speed is derived because it depends on distance and time, which are base quantities.

notes.title: SI units and prefixes
notes.answer: The SI unit of mass is the kilogram (kg).
notes.explanation: SI units give people around the world a common way to measure. Base units are the starting units; derived units are made from them. Prefixes show powers of ten, making very large or very small measurements easier to write.
notes.simple: Think of base units as the basic building blocks. Derived units combine those blocks, and prefixes tell you how many powers of ten a unit represents.
examples: Area = length × breadth = metre × metre = square metre = m².
steps: Name the physical quantity and identify its unit.
For a derived unit, write how the quantity is made from other quantities.
Replace each quantity with its SI base unit.
For a prefix, replace it with its power of ten and convert.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the SI unit and symbol for mass?
notes.checkAnswer: The unit of area is the square metre, m².

notes.title: Writing numbers in scientific notation
notes.answer: A number written as a number from 1 to 9 multiplied by a power of 10.
notes.explanation: Scientific notation writes a number as a value from 1 to 9 multiplied by a power of 10. The power shows how far, and in which direction, the decimal point moved.
notes.simple: Move the decimal point until one non-zero digit is left of it. Moving left gives a positive power; moving right gives a negative power.
steps: Move the decimal point until one non-zero digit remains on the left.
Count the places the decimal point moved.
Use that count as the exponent of 10: positive if the decimal moved left, negative if it moved right.

notes.title: Measuring length accurately
notes.explanation: To measure length accurately, choose an instrument with a suitable least count, line it up correctly with the object, and read the scale with your eye directly above it. For smaller objects, Vernier Callipers and a micrometer screw gauge give more precise readings than a metre rule.
notes.simple: Least count tells you the smallest length an instrument can measure accurately. Keep your eye straight above the scale so the reading does not look different.
examples: For the Vernier Callipers example: 4.3 cm + (0.01 cm × 4) = 4.34 cm.
For the screw gauge example: 6.5 mm + (25 × 0.01 mm) = 6.75 mm.
steps: Choose the instrument that suits the size of the object.
Place the object correctly and make sure the scale starts from the object's edge.
Read the scale with your eye directly above it to avoid parallax error.
For Vernier Callipers or a screw gauge, combine the main scale reading with the smaller scale reading multiplied by the least count.
Check for zero error and correct the observed reading as required.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the least count of the Vernier Callipers described in this section?
notes.checkAnswer: The least count is the smallest measurement that can be taken accurately with an instrument.

notes.title: Measuring Mass with a Physical Balance
notes.answer: The total of the standard masses on the right pan gives the mass of the object on the left pan.
notes.explanation: A physical balance measures mass by comparing an object with known standard masses. Put the object on the left pan and standard masses on the right pan. When the pointer stays at zero or oscillates equally on both sides of zero, add the standard masses to find the object's mass.
notes.simple: A physical balance finds mass by balancing an object against known masses.
examples: If the balance is level when a 20 g mass and a 5 g mass are on the right pan, the object on the left pan has a mass of 25 g.
A spring balance measures weight, which is a force; a physical balance is used to compare masses.
steps: Level the base using the levelling screws until the plumb line is exactly above the pointed mark.
Raise the pans and make sure the beam is horizontal and the pointer is at the centre of the scale. Adjust the balancing screws if needed.
Place the object on the left pan.
Use forceps to place known masses from the weight box on the right pan.
Adjust the masses until the pointer stays on zero or oscillates equally on both sides of zero.
Add the standard masses on the right pan. Their total is the mass of the object.
notes.checkQuestion: When the pointer is balanced, how do you find the object's mass?
notes.checkAnswer: The total of the standard masses on the right pan is the mass of the object on the left pan.

notes.title: Measuring time with a stopwatch
notes.answer: A mechanical stopwatch measures an event's duration, and its least count is one tenth of a second.
notes.explanation: A stopwatch measures how long an event lasts. A mechanical stopwatch in this section has a least count of one tenth of a second. A digital stopwatch can measure one hundredth of a second.
notes.simple: Use a stopwatch to measure how long something takes. Its least count tells you the smallest time interval it can measure.
steps: Press the knob to start the stopwatch.
Press the same knob to stop it when the event ends.
Read the time shown by the needles.
Press the knob again to return the needles to zero.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the least count of the mechanical stopwatch described in this section?
notes.checkAnswer: One tenth of a second (0.1 s).

notes.title: Measuring the volume of liquids and solids
notes.answer: For water, read the volume at the bottom edge of the meniscus, with your eye level with it.
notes.explanation: To measure liquid volume, place the measuring cylinder on a horizontal surface and read the meniscus at eye level. For water, read the bottom edge of the meniscus. To find the volume of a solid that does not dissolve, compare the liquid reading before and after immersing it. If the solid is too large for the cylinder, use a displacement can and measure the overflow.
notes.simple: Read the water level straight on, at the bottom of its curved surface. A solid’s volume is the amount of water it displaces.
examples: If the water level rises from 20 mL to 32 mL after a solid is immersed, the solid’s volume is 32 mL − 20 mL = 12 mL.
If a solid does not fit in a measuring cylinder, collect the overflow from a displacement can and measure it with a measuring cylinder.
steps: Place the measuring cylinder on a horizontal surface.
Bring your eye level with the water meniscus.
Read the scale at the bottom edge of the water meniscus.
To find a solid’s volume, subtract the initial liquid reading from the reading after the solid is immersed.
If the solid does not fit in the cylinder, collect the overflow from a displacement can and measure it in a measuring cylinder.
notes.checkQuestion: When reading the volume of water in a measuring cylinder, which edge of the meniscus should you read?
notes.checkAnswer: Read the bottom edge of the water meniscus with your eye level with it.

notes.title: Errors in Measurements
notes.answer: The three types of experimental errors are human errors, systematic errors and random errors.
notes.explanation: Measurements can be affected by human, systematic and random errors. Human errors come from the person taking the measurement; systematic errors affect readings consistently; random errors make repeated readings differ unpredictably.
notes.simple: Errors are differences between measured values and the true values. We identify the type of error by asking what caused it and how it affects the readings.
examples: A balance that is not properly calibrated causes a systematic error.
Air current making a balance fluctuate causes a random error.
steps: Look for the cause of the error.
If it comes from the person reading or handling the instrument, identify it as human error.
If a definite cause affects readings consistently, identify it as systematic error.
If repeated readings vary unpredictably, identify it as random error.
notes.checkQuestion: A balance has not been properly calibrated. What type of error can it cause?

notes.title: Uncertainty in a Measurement
notes.answer: For a metre rule with 0.1 cm smallest divisions, the maximum uncertainty is ±0.05 cm.
notes.explanation: Every measurement has some uncertainty, because an instrument cannot measure beyond the precision allowed by its smallest division. For an analogue scale, the maximum uncertainty is usually half the smallest division. Repeated readings and an average can reduce uncertainty.
notes.simple: A measurement is not perfectly exact. The instrument limits how certain the reading can be.
examples: A metre rule has a smallest division of 0.1 cm, so the maximum uncertainty is ±0.05 cm.
If a digital instrument's last digit fluctuates, that fluctuation shows uncertainty in the reading.
steps: Find the instrument's smallest division.
For the metre-rule example, divide 0.1 cm by 2.
State the maximum uncertainty as ±0.05 cm.
notes.checkQuestion: A scale has a smallest division of 0.1 cm. What is the maximum uncertainty?

notes.title: Counting Significant Figures
notes.answer: Significant figures are the reliably known digits in a measurement, including the first doubtful digit.
notes.explanation: Significant figures show which digits in a measurement are reliably known, including the first doubtful digit. Count all digits from 1 to 9. A zero between non-zero digits counts, a zero at the left does not, and a zero at the right of a decimal does. In scientific notation, count the digits before the exponent.
notes.simple: Significant figures are the measurement digits we can rely on, plus the first estimated digit. Count carefully: some zeros count and some do not.
examples: 5.06 m has 3 significant figures.
0.0034 m has 2 significant figures.
steps: Count all digits from 1 to 9.
Count a zero between two digits.
Do not count zeros on the left side of a measured value.
Count zeros on the right side of a decimal.
In scientific notation, count all digits before the exponent.
notes.checkQuestion: How many significant figures are there in 0.0034 m?

notes.title: Precision and Accuracy
notes.answer: They are precise, but not accurate.
notes.explanation: Precision tells us how close repeated measurements are to one another. Accuracy tells us how close a measured value is to the accepted or true value. A measurement can be precise without being accurate, accurate without being precise, both, or neither.
notes.simple: Precision is about measurements agreeing with each other. Accuracy is about a measurement agreeing with the true value.
examples: Arrows clustered together but away from the bullseye are precise, but not accurate.
A measurement of 2.00 cm is more precise than 2 cm because it is recorded to a smaller scale division; whether it is accurate depends on the true value.
steps: Compare repeated readings with one another to judge precision.
Compare the measured value with the accepted or true value to judge accuracy.
Remember: a smaller least count gives a more precise measurement.
A larger number of significant figures reflects higher accuracy.
notes.checkQuestion: A group of readings are very close to one another but all far from the true value. Are they precise, accurate, both, or neither?
notes.checkAnswer: Precision: repeated measurements are close together. Accuracy: a measurement is close to the accepted or true value.

notes.title: Rounding off to significant figures
notes.explanation: To round a number to a given number of significant figures, keep the required digits and use the next digit to decide whether to change the last kept digit. If the next digit is 5, use the rule in your textbook: an odd last kept digit goes up by one, while an even one stays the same.
notes.simple: Keep the digits you need. Look at the next digit to decide what happens to the last digit you keep.
examples: 3.4567 × 10⁴ kg rounded to 3 significant figures is 3.46 × 10⁴ kg.
4.45 × 10² m rounded to 2 significant figures is 4.4 × 10² m.
steps: Choose how many significant figures to keep.
Look at the first digit that will be left out.
If it is greater than 5, increase the last kept digit by 1; if it is less than 5, keep it unchanged.
If the digit is exactly 5, use the odd/even rule given in your textbook.
Write the rounded number with its original power of ten and unit.
notes.checkQuestion: Round off to 2 significant figures: 4.55 × 10² m.

notes.title: Measuring physical quantities
notes.answer: A measurement consists of a numerical value and a unit.
notes.explanation: Measurements use numbers and units. This chapter explains how to choose units and instruments, record readings carefully, use prefixes and scientific notation, and handle errors and significant digits.
notes.simple: A measurement tells how much of something there is. It needs a number and a unit.
examples: A desk height may be measured in metres (m).
A thickness may be measured with a micrometer screw gauge.
steps: Choose the quantity to measure.
Choose an appropriate instrument and unit.
Read the instrument carefully, avoiding viewing errors.
Record the number with its unit.
Use prefixes or scientific notation when useful.
notes.checkQuestion: Why do we need a standard unit for measurements?
notes.checkAnswer: A standard unit lets different people compare measurements consistently.

Correct: the projecting tail or depth gauge is used to measure depth.
A circular scale is part of the screw gauge, not the depth-measuring part of Vernier Callipers.

quiz.stem: A screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on its circular scale. What is its least count?
rationales: Correct: least count = pitch ÷ divisions = 0.5 mm ÷ 50 = 0.01 mm.
This is ten times the calculated least count.
This is not the pitch divided by the number of circular-scale divisions.
This is the pitch, not the least count.

quiz.stem: A Vernier Callipers has its Vernier zero to the right of the main-scale zero when its jaws are closed. How should its zero error be corrected?
options: Subtract the zero error from the observed measurement.
Add the zero error to the observed measurement.
Multiply the observed measurement by the zero error.
rationales: Correct: the instrument reads slightly more than the actual length, so subtract the zero error.
Adding it would make the reading still larger and less accurate.
The section gives correction by addition or subtraction, not multiplication.
Ignoring a zero error leaves the observed measurement uncorrected.

quiz.stem: Which method is used to find a screw-gauge measurement?
options: Read the sleeve just before the thimble, then add circular-scale reading × least count.
Multiply the sleeve reading by the circular-scale reading.
Subtract the sleeve reading from the circular-scale reading.
rationales: Correct: the reading is the main-scale reading plus circular-scale reading multiplied by the least count.
The two readings are not multiplied together.
The section does not calculate the measurement by subtracting these readings.
The main-scale reading must also be included.

quiz.stem: What least count is given for the micrometer screw gauge in this section?
rationales: This is the least count of the Vernier Callipers described in the section.
This is the least count of the metre rule and measuring tape in the section.
Correct: the screw gauge's least count is 0.01 mm.
This is the screw gauge pitch in the described example, not its least count.

quiz.stem: Which instrument is used in a laboratory to compare an object with known standard masses?
rationales: Correct: a physical balance compares an object with standard masses.
A spring balance measures weight, which is a force.
A metre rule measures length.
A measuring cylinder is used to measure liquid volume.

quiz.stem: What does mass measure?
options: The quantity of matter in a body
The force by which Earth attracts a body
The space occupied by a body
rationales: Correct: mass is the measure of the quantity of matter in a body.
This describes weight, not mass.
This describes volume.
This describes a length measurement.

quiz.stem: Which instrument can be used to measure the weight of a body?
rationales: Correct: weight is a force and can be measured using a spring balance.
A physical balance compares masses.
A metre rule measures length.
A stopwatch measures time.

quiz.stem: According to the textbook's procedure, where is the object placed on a physical balance?
rationales: Correct: the object to be weighed is placed on the left pan.
The known masses are placed on the right pan.
The procedure specifies a particular pan for the object.
The object must be placed on a pan to be weighed.

quiz.stem: How should known masses be placed in the right pan?
rationales: Correct: the procedure says to use forceps to place known masses from the weight box.
A metre rule is not used to transfer or measure the standard masses.
The textbook procedure specifies using forceps.
A spring balance measures weight and is not used to place standard masses.

quiz.stem: What indicates that the object and standard masses are balanced?
options: It stays on zero or oscillates equally on both sides of zero.
It remains at the end of the scale.
It moves only to the left of zero.
It stops moving while the pans are raised.
rationales: Correct: the pointer should remain on zero or oscillate equally on both sides of zero.
The pointer at the end of the scale does not indicate balance.
Movement only to one side indicates an unbalanced beam.
The textbook checks the pointer's position or equal oscillations, not merely whether it stops.

quiz.stem: What is the least count of the mechanical stopwatch described in this section?
rationales: This is correct: each small division represents one tenth of a second.
This is incorrect: one second is larger than the smallest division described.
This is incorrect: one hundredth of a second is the capability stated for digital watches, not this mechanical stopwatch.
This is incorrect: ten seconds is not the value of one small division.

quiz.stem: How is the dial of the mechanical stopwatch usually divided?
options: 30 big divisions, each divided into 10 small divisions
10 big divisions, each divided into 30 small divisions
30 small divisions, each divided into 10 big divisions
100 big divisions, each divided into 30 small divisions
rationales: This is correct: the section describes 30 big divisions, each further divided into 10 small divisions.
This is incorrect: it reverses the numbers of big and small divisions.
This is incorrect: it reverses which divisions are big and small.
This is incorrect: these are not the divisions described for the dial.

quiz.stem: What is a stopwatch used to measure?
options: It measures the duration of an event.
It measures the mass of an object.
It measures the length of an object.
It measures the temperature of a substance.
rationales: This is correct: a stopwatch measures how long an event lasts.
This is incorrect: a stopwatch does not measure mass.
This is incorrect: a stopwatch does not measure length.
This is incorrect: a stopwatch does not measure temperature.

quiz.stem: What part of a second can the electronic or digital watches mentioned in the section measure?
rationales: This is correct: the section says they can measure one hundredth part of a second.
This is incorrect: one tenth of a second is the mechanical stopwatch's least count.
This is incorrect: one second is not the smallest interval stated for the digital watches.
This is incorrect: one minute is much longer than the interval stated.

quiz.stem: How is the mechanical stopwatch started and stopped, according to the section?
options: The knob is pressed to start and pressed again to stop it.
The knob is pressed once to start and the needles stop by themselves.
The knob is turned continuously to keep the stopwatch running.
The stopwatch is shaken to start and stop it.
rationales: This is correct: pressing the knob starts the watch, and pressing it again stops it.
This is incorrect: the section says the same knob is pushed to stop it.
This is incorrect: the section does not describe turning the knob continuously.
This is incorrect: shaking the stopwatch is not the stated method.

quiz.stem: Which instrument in the section uses sand flowing from one chamber into another to indicate time?
rationales: This is correct: the sandclock uses sand flowing down from its upper chamber.
This is incorrect: a metre rule measures length, not time using flowing sand.
This is incorrect: a measuring cylinder measures volume, not time using flowing sand.
This is incorrect: a micrometer screw gauge measures small lengths, not time using flowing sand.

quiz.stem: Which instrument is designed to measure the volume of liquids and non-dissolvable solids?
options: A graduated glass or transparent plastic cylinder
A balance with a graduated scale
A ruler with a curved surface
A wide can with no scale
rationales: Correct: a measuring cylinder is a graduated cylinder used to measure liquid volume and the volume of non-dissolvable solids.
A balance measures mass, not volume.
A ruler measures length, not volume.
A can without a scale cannot directly give a volume reading.

quiz.stem: Where should the volume of water be read in a measuring cylinder?
options: At the top edge of the water meniscus
At the bottom edge of the water meniscus
At the middle of the water meniscus
At any point on the scale
rationales: The top edge is used for a convex mercury surface, not the concave surface of water.
Correct: the reading for water is taken at the bottom edge of its concave surface.
The book’s method specifies the bottom edge, not the middle.
The reading must correspond to the correct edge of the meniscus.

quiz.stem: How should the eye be positioned to read a measuring cylinder correctly?
options: Look down at the meniscus from above
Look up at the meniscus from below
Keep the eye level with the meniscus
Move the eye while taking the reading
rationales: Looking down at the meniscus gives an incorrect reading.
Looking up at it also gives an incorrect reading.
Correct: the eye should be level with the meniscus to avoid a viewing-angle error.
Moving the eye does not provide a reliable reading.

quiz.stem: What should you do with a measuring cylinder before taking a volume reading?
options: Place it on a horizontal surface
Keep it in the hand while reading
Place it on a sloping surface
rationales: Correct: the cylinder should be placed on a horizontal surface for a correct reading.
An angled cylinder can make the liquid level and scale reading unreliable.
Holding the cylinder can tilt it and disturb the reading.
A sloping surface does not provide the required level position.

quiz.stem: How is the volume of a non-dissolvable solid found by immersing it in liquid in a measuring cylinder?
options: Read the level after immersion only
Subtract the initial reading from the reading after immersion
rationales: The initial reading alone is the liquid’s volume before the solid is added.
The final reading includes both the liquid and the displaced volume, so it is not the solid’s volume alone.
Correct: the increase in the liquid reading equals the volume of the immersed solid.
Adding the readings does not give the volume of the solid.

quiz.stem: When is a displacement can especially useful for measuring a solid’s volume?
options: A solid that dissolves in the liquid
A solid that does not fit into a measuring cylinder
A liquid whose volume is already known
A solid that floats above the water
rationales: A dissolving solid changes the liquid and is not suitable for the displacement method described.
Correct: the section recommends a displacement can when the body does not fit into the measuring cylinder.
A displacement can is not needed simply because a liquid’s volume is known.
Floating does not by itself make the solid too large for the cylinder.

quiz.stem: In the displacement can method, what is collected in a beaker and measured with a measuring cylinder?
options: The liquid collected from the side opening
rationales: Correct: the overflowing liquid is collected and measured; its volume equals the solid’s volume.
The method measures volume, not mass.
The method does not require measuring the can’s capacity.
The method does not measure the body’s height.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes the correct reading of water in a measuring cylinder?
options: Water curves upward, so its top edge is read
Water curves downward, so its bottom edge is read
Water must be read from below the cylinder
rationales: Water curves downward; a top-edge reading is not the method given for water.
Correct: water has a concave surface that curves downward, and the reading is taken at its bottom edge.
Water has a meniscus, which is the top level of the liquid surface.
The eye should be level with the meniscus, not below the cylinder.

quiz.stem: A student reads a scale while looking at it from an angle. What type of error is most likely?
rationales: Correct: the error is caused by the student's way of reading the scale.
Incorrect: no definite instrument fault affecting readings consistently is described.
Incorrect: unpredictable variation between repeated readings is not described.
Incorrect: looking from an angle can cause an incorrect reading.

quiz.stem: A balance has a zero error that shifts every reading by the same amount. This is a:
rationales: Incorrect: the cause is an instrument fault, not the user's reading or handling.
Correct: a zero error gives a consistent effect on measurements.
Incorrect: the error is not an unpredictable variation between readings.
Incorrect: a correction factor may be used to reduce an error, but it is not a type of error.

quiz.stem: Repeated measurements differ unpredictably because the room temperature keeps changing. This is a:
rationales: Incorrect: the stated cause is environmental variation, not personal performance.
Incorrect: no consistent shift affecting all readings equally is described.
Correct: unpredictable changes in environmental conditions can cause random errors.
Incorrect: taking an average is a way to reduce random error, not a type of error.

quiz.stem: Which method helps reduce the effect of random errors?
options: Use several readings and find their mean
Read the scale from different directions
Ignore all readings except the largest
rationales: Correct: averaging several readings helps reduce the effect of random variation.
Incorrect: changing the viewing direction can introduce reading errors rather than reduce random errors.
Incorrect: choosing only the largest reading does not give a reliable average.
Incorrect: changing the quantity does not reduce errors in its measurement.

quiz.stem: Which action can help reduce human errors?
options: Use an instrument with an unknown zero error
Read the scale from an angle
rationales: Correct: proper training and technique help prevent errors caused by personal performance.
Incorrect: one reading does not prevent a person from making a reading error.
Incorrect: an unknown zero error is an instrument problem and can cause systematic error.
Incorrect: reading from an angle can cause a personal reading error.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes systematic error?
options: It affects readings consistently because of a definite cause
It occurs only when repeated values are different
It is always caused by the experimenter's reaction time
rationales: Correct: systematic error arises from a definite cause and produces a consistent effect.
Incorrect: different repeated values under the same conditions describe random error.
Incorrect: reaction time is an example of human error, not the definition of systematic error.
Incorrect: systematic error can be reduced, for example by comparing with a more accurate instrument and applying a correction.

quiz.stem: A metre rule has a smallest division of 0.1 cm. What is the maximum uncertainty in a reading?
rationales: This is the full smallest division, not half of it.
The maximum uncertainty is half the smallest division: 0.1 cm ÷ 2 = 0.05 cm.
This is smaller than half the smallest division.
This is greater than the smallest division of the rule.

quiz.stem: What sets a limit to the accuracy that can be achieved with a measuring instrument?
rationales: The smallest division of the instrument limits the degree of accuracy possible.
The object's mass does not determine the instrument's scale resolution.
The total length of the scale does not set the precision of each reading.
The number of readings can help reduce uncertainty but does not set the instrument's scale limit.

quiz.stem: On a digital instrument, uncertainty is often shown by fluctuation in which part of the reading?
rationales: The first digit is not usually the digit that fluctuates to show uncertainty.
The last digit commonly fluctuates and indicates the uncertain part of the digital reading.
A unit symbol does not fluctuate as part of the measured value.
The textbook describes fluctuation in the last digit, not equal changes in every digit.

quiz.stem: How can uncertainty in a short time interval be reduced?
options: Take several readings and find their average
rationales: One reading does not use repeated measurements to reduce uncertainty.
Taking multiple readings and finding the average can reduce uncertainty.
Rounding every reading up introduces a bias rather than reducing uncertainty.
Changing the unit does not itself reduce uncertainty.

quiz.stem: Which activity is excluded from the textbook's statement that measurements have inevitable uncertainty?
rationales: The text says uncertainty applies whenever a physical quantity is measured except counting.
A wire's diameter is measured and can have uncertainty.
A time interval is measured and can have uncertainty.
A length is measured and can have uncertainty.

quiz.stem: Why are significant figures useful in measurements?
options: They show the uncertainty or accuracy of a measured quantity conveniently
They remove all uncertainty from a measurement
They change the instrument's smallest division
They are used only for digital instruments
rationales: The textbook says significant figures conveniently indicate uncertainty or accuracy in a measured value.
Significant figures do not make any measurement perfectly certain.
Writing significant figures does not change the instrument's scale.
Significant figures are not restricted to digital instruments.

quiz.stem: How many significant figures are in 0.00620 m?
rationales: This is incorrect because the leading zeros do not count, but the final decimal zero does.
This is correct: 6, 2 and the final decimal zero are significant.
This is incorrect because the zeros before 6 are not significant.
This is incorrect because there are only three significant digits.

quiz.stem: What does precision of a measurement describe?
options: How close repeated measurements are to one another
How close a measured value is to the true value
The unit used to record a measurement
The size of the object being measured
rationales: This is correct because precision describes how close a group of measurements is to one another.
This describes accuracy, not precision.
A unit does not by itself describe the precision of a measurement.
The object's size is not the definition of precision.

quiz.stem: Which description best represents measurements that are precise but not accurate?
options: Readings close together but far from the true value
Readings spread out but centred around the true value
One reading recorded with many decimal places
rationales: This is correct: the readings agree with one another but are not near the true value.
This suggests accuracy without precision, if their centre is near the true value.
Zero readings do not establish either precision or accuracy without knowing the true value.
Many decimal places alone do not guarantee precision or accuracy.

quiz.stem: According to this section, what makes an instrument give a more precise measurement?
rationales: This is correct because the section says the smaller the least count, the more precise the measurement.
A larger least count gives less precise readings.
The object's size does not determine the instrument's precision.
The time spent measuring does not itself determine the instrument's least count.

quiz.stem: Which feature reflects the accuracy of a measurement in this section?
options: The number of units in a measurement
rationales: This is correct: the section says accuracy is reflected by the number of significant figures.
Instrument colour has no bearing on accuracy.
Object length alone does not show how accurate its measurement is.
The number of units is not the stated indicator of accuracy.

quiz.stem: Which statement is the best description of accuracy?
options: Repeated readings are close to one another
A measured value is close to the accepted value
An instrument has a small least count
The measurement is written in a table
rationales: This describes precision.
This is correct because accuracy is closeness to an accepted or true value.
A small least count improves precision, but is not the definition of accuracy.
Writing a measurement in a table does not establish its accuracy.

quiz.stem: Which timing device in Table 1.7 measures short time intervals to an accuracy of ±0.01 s?
rationales: This is correct: the table gives the digital stopwatch an accuracy of ±0.01 s.
The table gives the analogue stopwatch an accuracy of ±0.1 s.
The table lists a watch or clock for longer intervals, not this stated accuracy.
The atomic clock measures very short intervals of about 10⁻¹⁰ seconds; the table does not give it the stated ±0.01 s accuracy.

quiz.stem: According to the section, which measurement generally reflects higher accuracy?
options: A larger number of significant figures
A smaller number of significant figures
A unit with a longer name
rationales: This is correct: the section states that a larger number of significant figures reflects higher accuracy.
This is opposite to what the section states.
The size of the object does not itself indicate the accuracy of its measurement.
The length of a unit's name has no connection to accuracy.

quiz.stem: What does the section say about measuring a small physical quantity?
options: The smaller the quantity, the more precise an instrument is needed
The smaller the quantity, the less precise an instrument is needed
Every quantity must be measured with the same instrument
Precision depends only on the object's material
rationales: This is correct: the section states that a smaller physical quantity needs a more precise instrument.
This reverses the relationship described in the section.
Different quantities and sizes can require different instruments.
The object's material is not stated as the factor that determines precision.

quiz.stem: What is 2.512 × 10³ m rounded to 2 significant figures?
rationales: Correct: the first two significant figures are 2 and 5, and the next digit is 1, so the 5 stays unchanged.
This keeps three significant figures, not two.
The next digit is less than 5, so the 5 should not increase.
This does not follow the required significant-figure rounding.

quiz.stem: Round 3.4567 × 10⁴ kg to 3 significant figures.
rationales: This would require the next digit to be less than 5, but it is 6.
Correct: the first three significant figures are 3, 4 and 5; the next digit is 6, so the 5 increases to 6.
This has only two significant figures.
The first significant digit is 3, not 4.

quiz.stem: According to the odd/even rule in your textbook, what is 4.45 × 10² m rounded to 2 significant figures?
rationales: Correct: the last retained digit is 4, which is even, so it remains unchanged.
The last retained digit is even, so it does not increase.
This answer has three significant figures.
This is not the result of applying the stated rounding rule.

quiz.stem: According to the odd/even rule in your textbook, what is 4.55 × 10² m rounded to 2 significant figures?
rationales: The last retained digit is 5, which is odd, so it must increase.
Correct: the last retained digit 5 is odd, so it increases to 6.
This has three significant figures and is not rounded to two.
This is not the result of applying the stated rule.

quiz.stem: Your textbook rounds 4.452 × 10² m to 2 significant figures using the closeness of the number to the nearest value. What is the result?
rationales: The textbook explains that 4.452 is closer to 4.5 than to 4.4.
Correct: 4.452 is closer to 4.5 than to 4.4.
This has three significant figures.
This is not the nearest value to 4.452 at 2 significant figures.

quiz.stem: Q1.1. The instrument that is most suitable for measuring the thickness of a few sheets of cardboard is:
rationales: A metre rule is not precise enough for a few sheets.
A measuring tape is intended for larger lengths.
Vernier Callipers can measure small thicknesses but are less suitable than a micrometer for this very small thickness.
A micrometer screw gauge is the most suitable choice for measuring a small thickness precisely.

quiz.stem: Q1.2. One femtometre is equal to:
rationales: 10⁻⁹ m is a nanometre, not a femtometre.
The prefix femto means 10⁻¹⁵.
10⁹ m is not the femto scale.
10¹⁵ m is not the femto scale.

quiz.stem: Q1.3. A light year is a unit of:
rationales: A light year is not a measure of light itself.
A year is a time interval, but a light year is not a time unit.
A light year is the distance light travels in one year.
Speed is distance per unit time, not a light year.

quiz.stem: Q1.4. Which one is a non-physical quantity?
rationales: Distance is measurable, so it is physical.
Density is measurable, so it is physical.
Colour, as stated here, is not a physical quantity measured as a numerical quantity with a unit.
Temperature is measurable, so it is physical.

quiz.stem: Q1.5. When using a measuring cylinder, one precaution to take is to:
options: look at the meniscus from below the level of the water surface
take several readings by looking from more than one direction
position the eye in line with the bottom of the meniscus
rationales: Zero error is not the precaution being tested for a measuring cylinder reading here.
Looking from below the surface causes a viewing error.
Looking from different directions does not give a correct meniscus reading.
The eye should be in line with the bottom of the meniscus to avoid parallax error.

quiz.stem: Q1.6. Volume of water consumed by you per day is estimated in:
rationales: A millilitre is too small a convenient unit for a daily amount.
A litre is an appropriate unit for daily water consumption.
A kilogram is a unit of mass, not volume.
A cubic metre is much too large for this estimate.

quiz.stem: Q1.7. A displacement can is used to measure:
rationales: A displacement can does not measure mass.
A displacement can does not measure mass.
It is used to find the volume of an irregular solid by displacement, not the volume of a liquid.
The displaced liquid gives the volume of a solid.

quiz.stem: Q1.8. Two rods with lengths 12.321 cm and 10.3 cm are placed side by side, the difference in their lengths is:
rationales: The subtraction is 2.021 cm, but the result should be rounded to the least precise decimal place, tenths.
12.321 − 10.3 = 2.021 cm, rounded to one decimal place gives 2.0 cm.
2 cm loses the tenths place required by the measurement rule.
2.021 cm reports unjustified precision.

quiz.stem: Q1.9. Four students measure the diameter of a cylinder with Vernier Callipers. Which of the following readings is correct?
rationales: This does not report the reading to the appropriate precision.
This gives too many decimal places for the usual Vernier Callipers reading shown by the choices.
3.47 cm is the reading expressed to the appropriate precision.
3.5 cm is too coarsely recorded.

quiz.stem: Q1.10. Which of the following measures are likely to represent the thickness of a sheet of this book?
rationales: This is far too small for a book sheet.
10⁻⁴ m is a plausible sheet thickness.
This is a nuclear-scale length and far too small.
This is 4 cm, far too thick for a sheet.

quiz.stem: Q1.11. In a Vernier Callipers ten smallest divisions of the Vernier scale are equal to nine smallest divisions of the main scale. If the smallest division of the main scale is half millimetre, the Vernier constant is equal to:
rationales: 0.5 mm is one main-scale division, not the Vernier constant.
One Vernier division is 0.45 mm, so the difference is 0.05 mm, not 0.1 mm.
One main-scale division is 0.5 mm; one Vernier division is 9 × 0.5 ÷ 10 = 0.45 mm, so the difference is 0.05 mm.
0.001 mm is too small and does not follow from the given scales.
